dossiers.label: Aristophanes' myth of the split humans
dossiers.about: Our original nature: round double beings of three sexes, male, female and androgynous, who assaulted the gods; Zeus cut them in two like sorb-apples, and love is the longing of each half for its other, the desire and pursuit of the whole.

passage.start_quote: ἄλλῃ γέ πῃ ἐν νῷ ἔχω λέγειν ἢ ᾗ σύ τε καὶ Παυσανίας εἰπέτην
passage.end_quote: οὗτος, ἔφη, ὦ Ἐρυξίμαχε, ὁ ἐμὸς λόγος ἐστὶ περὶ Ἔρωτος

parts.label: Our ancient nature was not the same as now
Three kinds: male, female and androgynous
Each of us a tally, like a flatfish
Love is the name for the desire and pursuit of the whole

echoes.why: Diotima answers: love is not of the half nor of the whole, unless it is good.
After Socrates' speech Aristophanes tries to reply to Socrates' allusion to him.

related.why: Diotima corrects Aristophanes: love is not of the half or the whole but of the good.

dossiers.label: The birth of Eros: Poros and Penia
dossiers.about: Diotima's story: at the feast for Aphrodite's birth, Poverty lay with the drunken Resource and conceived Eros, who is neither god nor mortal, neither wise nor ignorant, but a daimon between, a lover of wisdom.

passage.end_quote: τοιοῦτος ὢν ὁ Ἔρως τίνα χρείαν ἔχει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις

parts.label: Resource, son of Cunning, at the feast
Poverty conceives a child by him
parts.quote: ἡ οὖν Πενία ἐπιβουλεύουσα διὰ τὴν αὑτῆς ἀπορίαν παιδίον ποιήσασθαι ἐκ τοῦ Πόρου

parts.label: Eros a philosopher, between wisdom and ignorance

echoes.quote: μεταξύ ἐστι θεοῦ τε καὶ θνητοῦ
echoes.why: Just before: everything daimonic is between god and mortal.

web.title: Symposium (Plato)
web.quote: upon seeing Porus lying unconscious took the chance to sleep with him

dossiers.label: The ladder of love
dossiers.about: Diotima's 'final mysteries': the lover rises from one beautiful body to all, to beautiful souls, practices and laws, to the sciences, and suddenly beholds beauty itself, always being, unmixed, in which all beautiful things share.

parts.label: Suddenly he will see something wonderful
Always being, neither coming to be nor perishing
parts.quote: ἀεὶ ὂν καὶ οὔτε γιγνόμενον οὔτε ἀπολλύμενον

parts.label: Giving birth to true virtue, dear to the gods

diagram.title: The steps of 211c
diagram.about: Diotima's own summary of the ascent at 211c, from the first step to the last, as rungs.

steps.label: to all beautiful bodies
steps.quote: ἀπὸ δυοῖν ἐπὶ πάντα τὰ καλὰ σώματα

steps.label: to beautiful practices
steps.quote: ἀπὸ τῶν καλῶν σωμάτων ἐπὶ τὰ καλὰ ἐπιτηδεύματα

steps.label: to beautiful learning
steps.quote: ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιτηδευμάτων ἐπὶ τὰ καλὰ μαθήματα

steps.label: to that learning which is of beauty itself
to know at last what beauty itself is

echoes.why: The Phaedrus: of the forms beauty alone shines clearly through sight.
The Republic: few can reach beauty itself and see it by itself.

related.why: In the Phaedrus too the sight of beauty regrows the soul's wings.
Both are ascents ending in a sudden sight of what is.

evidence.quote: τὴν δὲ ἄνω ἀνάβασιν καὶ θέαν τῶν ἄνω

testimonia.quote: the beauty in bodies, will then proceed to the beauty of the soul
testimonia.says: Alcinous retells the ascent of the Symposium as the way to think of the good.

dossiers.label: Socrates as a Silenus figure
dossiers.about: Alcibiades' praise of Socrates 'through images': he is like the Silenus statues in the sculptors' shops, which open to show images of gods inside, and like the satyr Marsyas, who bewitched with the flute as Socrates does with bare words.

passage.start_quote: ἔσται δʼ ἡ εἰκὼν τοῦ ἀληθοῦς ἕνεκα, οὐ τοῦ γελοίου

parts.label: The image is for the truth, not for a laugh
parts.quote: ἡ εἰκὼν τοῦ ἀληθοῦς ἕνεκα, οὐ τοῦ γελοίου

parts.label: Silenus figures with gods inside
parts.quote: διχάδε διοιχθέντες φαίνονται ἔνδοθεν ἀγάλματα ἔχοντες θεῶν

parts.label: His words, too, like the opened Silenus

echoes.why: Meno's comparison of Socrates to the torpedo fish, another likeness of his effect.

related.why: Another image of Socrates' effect on those he talks with.
